title: A vendor slips on a fixed-price contract
setting: Predictive project to fit out a new customer call centre for a regional water utility. Headsets and phone switches come from one vendor on a fixed-price contract with dated milestones and a written change-order clause.

steps.line: I'm Alex, assistant PM on the call-centre fit-out. Grace is the PM. Our schedule and cost baselines were approved last month.
The equipment vendor is on a fixed-price contract. Any change to price or scope needs a written change order signed by both sides.
Victor, the vendor's account lead, calls. The headset and switch install will be two weeks late because a part is back-ordered.
I message the training lead straight away and ask her to push all the agent training sessions back two weeks to match.

error.summary: Moved training dates before checking what the delay affects
error.why: The delay's real impact isn't known yet. Before changing any dates, check the schedule: is the install on the critical path, is there float, and what actually depends on it? Reacting first can create a slip that wasn't there.
error.correctAction: Hold the training dates, check the install's float and dependencies in the schedule, then agree any date change with Grace through the normal process.
error.consequence: The install had three weeks of float, so training never needed to move. The trainers were rebooked at a cancellation fee, and go-live slipped a week for no reason.

steps.line: I ask Victor to send a written recovery plan with the new dates, as the contract asks for when a milestone is late.
Victor offers to air-freight the part for an extra fee. I tell him yes, go ahead, and we'll sort out the paperwork afterwards.

error.summary: Agreed a price change on a fixed-price contract verbally
error.why: The contract says price changes need a signed change order, and an assistant PM has no authority to commit extra money. A verbal yes can bind the company, breaks the contract's own process, and skips the impact check.
error.correctAction: Thank Victor, ask him to put the offer in writing, and take it to Grace and the contracts officer to assess against the schedule and decide through a change order.
error.consequence: The vendor invoiced the air freight, citing Alex's call. Procurement refused to pay without a change order, the dispute went to legal, and the final milestone payment was frozen for two months.

steps.line: I log the delay in the issue log with Victor's reason, the dates, and the contract clause, so the facts are clear later.
I put the vendor delay at the bottom of my weekly status email, under other notes, below the good news.

error.summary: Buried bad news at the bottom of the status report
error.why: Bad news should be easy to see. Hiding a delay under other notes means Grace and the sponsor may miss it and lose time to respond. Status should lead with what needs attention.
error.correctAction: Put the delay at the top of the status update with its impact and next steps, and tell Grace directly before the email goes out.
error.consequence: The sponsor skimmed the email and told the board everything was on track. When the delay surfaced a week later, she asked why she hadn't been told.

steps.line: I book thirty minutes with Grace and the contracts officer to go through Victor's recovery plan and our options.
I add a risk for vendor supply problems, with Grace as owner, to be reviewed at every remaining milestone.
